title: Heart Sutra, Part 7: The Good News
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the last pages of the Heart Sutra chant, from the list of "no" lines through the closing mantra. Nomon proposes the Chinese word for sky in place of emptiness, since sky has room for all of the mind's weather, even storms. The "no" lines point to the twelvefold chain and the Four Noble Truths, and Nomon sets Dan Harris's 10 Percent Happier beside the Buddha's claim of full freedom from suffering. Nomon then explains the four inverted views, which no longer arise, much as a winged rabbit never comes to mind, and the mantra "gate, gate, para gate, parasam gate, bodhi svaha." The evening ends with trio conversations about what struck people in the sutra.

sentences.text: One more talk on the Heart Sutra, then I'll stop for now.
First, a side note: I hope you had a chance to greet our great first ancestor Bodhidharma on your way in.
If you didn't notice him, he's standing patiently waiting for you, just kind of by the front door in the corner of the building.
I don't even know the name of the donor, actually; it was organized by her friend, named Steve Givens.
Do you know Steve Givens?
Oh, and I guess she is a collector of Asian art, and she moved away from Kent and wanted Bodhidharma to go to a good home.
So check out Bodhidharma; it's a pretty detailed carving, amazing carving, really beautiful.
It was carved out of one big piece of wood, and he's really heavy too.
And hopefully, he's completed his journey.
So now we can have a co-on.
Why did Bodhidharma come from Kent?
Now, the red-bearded barbarian.
Some of you are here for some of the talks, or all of the talks maybe, on the Heart Sutra, which we just chanted, the first of three.
And fun, we're doing a couple more chants tonight than we have of late.
We've already talked a lot about the central point of the sutra, which is to appreciate emptiness.
This odd technical Buddhist term that translates as emptiness is a word that was used to point towards something much bigger than words.
It's the kind of wide-open, interpenetrated, fluid way things actually are, unlike the way we tend to think they are without really thinking about the way we're thinking.
We tend to lock things down: this is this, and this is that, and she's that way, and I'm this way.
We tend to assume that things are sort of inherently the way they are.
But the emptiness teachings say, "No, look again, look again, and look again," not just so you'll be in alignment with the credo or something.
But look again because that way of thinking creates rigidity and suffering and separateness.
We talked a lot about how the main thing that we have trouble not making into a solid something is our self, our idea of who we are.
That leads to all kind of trouble.
But what else does selfing inevitably lead to?
Othering, right?
If there's selfing, then there's othering.
We are certainly seeing in the bigger world, and if we pay attention, we see this every day around us, the effects of othering.
The great moments of joy and connection are when all that's more transparent, less prevalent, less strong, the boundaries are down, and trust and vulnerability are here.
There's not so much selfing and othering.
Those are the best moments, don't you think?
So it may be useful to have the chant book.
We're going to try to make a little progress tonight because it's kind of convenient the way we arrange the words in the chant book on page five and six.
Page five is pretty much all about emptiness, and we spent a lot of time on it, so we'll finish up page five.
Then page six is like a whole new section, a whole new theme.
It's kind of like, "Well, what are the beneficial results of all this?
Why is this a great thing?
And how do we really bring it home into our lives?"
First, another little side note about translation.
I am kind of fascinated by translation.
As you might have noticed, we in English directly and literally translated the Sanskrit term *sunyata* into emptiness.
The Chinese, who do have a perfectly good word that literally means emptiness, instead of using that word, used a word which pronounced something like *kong*, which actually means sky, like the sky.
So they were a little more poetic.
Maybe that would have been better for us—the sky-like quality of reality of each of ourselves, of each other.
We're vast like the sky.
So it would be kind of fun; you can kind of rewrite the sutra with that word if you want.
So, *form does not differ from sky.
The sky does not differ from form.
Form itself is sky.
Sky itself is form.
And everything is like this.* It's kind of fun, huh, to be the sky.
The sky, you know, is a great reality.
Good thing we have the sky, you know.
We're so grateful that we have an atmosphere, but also a wonderful metaphor for our mind.
We really embrace our mind as the sky, vast and open.
One of the things that's really great about the sky is the way it gives space for weather.
And we have lots of internal weather, right?
It can be sunny in there or kind of gray and drizzly.
It can be stormy.
There can be storms in the mind violent enough that they kill us, right?
Like literally; this has happened.
But the sky has room for all the weather, you know.
So emptiness is like that—so much room, space for everything.
When you feel like you're oppressed by the weather in your mind, and you're only seeing the darkness and the biting wind and the cold rain, it's horrible, you know.
Maybe sometimes you'll remember, and practice will help us with this.
Maybe sometimes you'll remember that behind even the thickest storm clouds, the worst storm—the hurricanes and typhoons and everything—behind all that always is the vast blue sky.
It's one of the great things sometimes about going on the airplane.
Have you ever had that experience on the airplane?
When you go up to thirty thousand feet and sometimes you fly above the weather.
You're doing a terrible thing for the climate, but it's really cool to be above the weather, and you remember that it's always true.
So the last paragraph on page five continues the use of negation to try to do something.
The Heart Sutra is really condensed, like mega-condensed.
They couldn't have made it any shorter if they tried, and maybe they did try.
Because in this whole section, from the fourth paragraph and now the fifth paragraph, the last paragraph on page five, the sutra runs through a list of things and says "no, no, no, no, no, no, no."
Here, "no" is not to say that that doesn't happen or there's no experience of that.
We know that we have eyes and ears and nose and all this.
We know that there are sights and sounds and smells and consciousness that arises from all this.
We have this experience.
The "no" here means this too is empty.
It's empty, and one way to read that "no," to hear that "no," is something like "is not really the way you think it is."
But that would be way too many words, right?
It would be hard to chant too.
So you can just go look at it that way: your eyes are not the way you think they are.
Your vision is not the way you think it is.
Your consciousness is not the way you think it is.
That paragraph, the fourth paragraph, is all about our experience of living, basically.
The last paragraph is about two major fundamental Buddhist teachings which are really useful.
The sutra is reminding us not to settle for our first impression, to practice them deeply, to go beyond what even it says in the book.
The first one here says, "There is neither ignorance nor extinction of ignorance, neither old age and death, nor extinction of old age and death."
So stop there.
In the middle, there is a dot, dot, dot, which leaves out a whole big pile of stuff, which we'll have to save for seven talks another time.
What that is is the first and last of a set of twelve steps that are all about how a moment of experience comes into existence and vanishes again.
It's called the twelve-fold chain of interdependent arising.
It's a really cool teaching, but I will be restrained about it.
But it basically says first there's a moment of awareness, and then this happens, and this happens, and this happens.
In the process of all that, you perceive things, you notice things, you have impulses about things.
In the standard way that things go, in that chain of twelve steps, there's clinging, there's grasping, there's pushing away, there's suffering.
It seemed really cool at first, but then the whole thing runs all over again, all over again.
So it sounds a little negative, but the Buddha is really trying to describe very systematically the way we get caught up, the way we get caught up in things.
Then he says the way to get uncaught up in things is to do that whole process in reverse.
Just run the thing backwards, run it back to zero, get back to the moment of experience, which is what we're doing in meditation.
That's the part about extinction.

That one little line with a couple of "nos" is to say you should carefully study this teaching, which we'll do another time, on how each moment comes to be and how people tend to respond and react and get caught by things, and how we do all this practice and try to unravel this whole chain and get back to the baseline, get back to peace.
That too, you know, that too we can go deeper.
That too is not the way you think it is.
No.
No.
And then the second half of this last paragraph is the most famous Buddhist teaching of all with a bunch of "nos."
I was reading one commentary on this last little section here where it says, "No suffering, no cause, no cessation, no path, no knowledge, and no attainment."
The author of that book, a modern author, was saying this must have been shocking.
This was really like stirring the pot.

The authors of this sutra and the sutras in its group called the Wisdom Sutras, Prajnaparamita Sutras, they must have really been trying to get a rise out of the earlier Buddhists, the more the traditionalists, the fundamentalists.
I feel like showing up in church and saying, "No God!"
A wise pastor would say, "Yeah, you're right, no God!
That's why we love God!"
But probably they wouldn't all pull that off.
Some would kick you out, probably.
So maybe there is an element of that here too, like wake up, don't get so comfortable with these teachings.
This last one is the famous Four Noble Truths, which is a really, really useful teaching—four things to think about in terms of how things unfold.
So we got a list of twelve, a list of four, five of this, different ways of unpacking our experience.
But these Four Noble Truths is just like the number one core teaching of Buddhism, and it's really sensible, actually.
The First Noble Truth is the truth of suffering.

Here the Buddha says, and I think it's hard to argue with these, that life where we're conditioned and believe we're separate and believe all the things that we believe is never going to be fully satisfying, right?
It'll have its good moments for sure, you know.
But at the end of the day, it's like, "Ah, why am I not content?
I have everything I need."
So this is a kind of suffering because we're kind of betting on the wrong horse.
We're leaning on something that's empty, right?
And wishing it were solid.
We want lasting satisfaction from things that aren't going to give us lasting satisfaction.
Check yourself out.
We all do this.
You just have to see how it is for you, not just like listen to it as an idea.
The Second Noble Truth is the truth of cause.
Here it says "no cause."
The Buddha pretty much figured out, and again I think it's true, that this sort of causal theme is grasping, is wanting things to be other than the way they actually are.
Maybe you want more of something that you are attracted to, or less of something you are repulsed by.
Maybe you wish for a world that was this way or that way, and this is reasonable; it would be great to have a better world.
But there's something about the way we tend to do this—that's sticky.
It's the stickiness.
So the Second Noble Truth is stickiness, you know.
Things get sticky for us.
The cause.
The traditional word that's used means thirst, our continuous thirst, unquenchable thirst.
So that's like the first two of the four are like the problem statement, and the second two are the solution.
So yeah, no worries, hang in there.
The Third Noble Truth is cessation, that this, even the most subtle and pervasive and hard to quite figure out what the heck is bothering you kinds of suffering, are not permanent either.
They too can stop.
They too can cease.
So here it says "no cessation" at the very bottom of page five.
"No cessation."
So there is cessation.
That's why there's "no cessation"—that it's possible; we're not stuck with this, you know?
These are powerful patterns.
It's not like some little thing like, "Oh yeah, I heard in the Tarot Man talk there's no suffering, I haven't suffered since."
It's really great, you know.
You should go to the Red Cedars Inn; they didn't even charge me.
No, right?
It's planting seeds for a lifetime of practice.
And it's not all or nothing either, right?
There can be a little less suffering, a little less thirst, a little more freedom, a little more cessation.
But Buddhism does not make a small claim either, though.
It doesn't say, "Yeah, you'll feel a little bit better."
There's a guy in the mindfulness space that I also work in, named Dan Harris.
You know about Dan Harris?
He's a good guy.
He was a news anchor, like a high, hard-charging, drug-using, stressed-out, mega-professional, top-of-his-game, making a gazillion bucks as a news anchor on TV.
And one day, on air, he choked.
He froze.
He couldn't get another word out, you know.
So he experienced some big suffering, and he ended up getting into meditation, much to his surprise.
And now he makes his living like running this meditation company.
That's kind of great.
But anyway, he has a modest claim, this guy Dan Harris.
His business and his app and his book and everything are called *10 Percent Happier*.
Yeah, 10 percent.
No, it's Dan Harris.
Sam Harris is another guy in the same world; he's the atheist guy, Sam Harris.
This is Dan Harris.
But anyway, 10 percent.
You know, first I saw that, I'm like, "That's...
Can I have more?"
But then you think about it, you're like, any significant change matters.
Like 10 percent, and then 10, maybe it's compounding interest. 10 percent.
But the Buddha does not say 10 percent.
He says 100 percent, you know?
Full freedom from suffering.
And then the fourth noble truth is the truth of the path.
Like, well, how do we practice this?
How do we get there?
And of course, emptiness says there's no there there, but we're still going, you know, we're still moving in that direction.
So anyway, the Heart Sutra, after describing our experience of ourselves in all kinds of different ways, is informed and then says again, even the core teachings of Buddhism are empty.
Even that, even that is not the way you think it is.
Even that, you can go deeper.
And then on page six, we get to the good news.
With nothing to attain, a bodhisattva relies on prajnaparamita, and thus the mind is without hindrance.
Without hindrance, there is no fear, far beyond all inverted views, and it realizes nirvana.
Suddenly, it does seem like a bit of a change of topic, though; we did mention prajnaparamita at the very beginning.
So that does kind of bring us full circle.
What is prajnaparamita?
Prajna literally means wisdom.
The bodhisattva, and we are bodhisattvas, are beings devoted to freedom and helping each other, so we are bodhisattvas, and they rely on wisdom.
They rely on understanding all this emptiness stuff, and paramita means kind of like a positive spin on emptiness.
Paramita means going beyond; it is a wisdom that goes beyond wisdom.
Maybe you remember hearing that a minute ago; it was the title we gave, the Heart Sutra, and it is right here too: wisdom beyond wisdom.

This is the same paramitas if you come to the Sunday meetings or listen during the talks online; these are the same paramitas that we have been talking about there, so it is all one tradition, it all fits together.
We do not rely on trying to get what we want and perfect ourselves; we let go of ourselves and we rely on wisdom.
This little phrase at the beginning here, "with nothing to attain," is not a throwaway phrase with nothing to attain.
If there was stuff, then we could attain it, right?
Stuff could include physical stuff, or mental stuff, or philosophical stuff—all kinds of stuff.
If there was stuff, we could attain it.
But if stuff is empty, then there is nothing to attain, right?
How can you attain something that is empty?
This is actually an incredibly wonderful thing; this is a radical kind of freedom to realize that there is nothing to attain.
To say "relies on prajnaparamita" actually means relies on nothing.
There is nothing to attain, and we rely on that.
We rely on that nothingness, that emptiness, and thus we are not stuck anymore, right?
The stickiness melts away, and when the stickiness melts away, there is nothing to be really afraid of.
This is not denial, though; this is not denial.
Bodhisattvas are still horrified by violence and inequity.
Bodhisattvas absolutely care about justice and love, but they take a stance that is sustainable—imperturbable.
They do not get knocked flat; they are sad, it is upsetting, but they can keep going because they can see how fluid and empty it all is and how temporary it is.

They do not have this problem that we tend to have of mistakenly thinking we can predict what is going to happen next, and usually our predictions are pretty terrible because past and future are also empty.
So the bodhisattvas just show up and do their best to help with nothing to attain, relying on nothing.
It says that what happens in their mind is they get beyond inverted views.
What are the inverted views?
It turns out there is another list.
Would you like to know what the four inverted views are?
Number one is the view that anything can ever be permanent; that is an upside-down view, inverted, upside-down, so believing in permanence.
This includes stuff we do without thinking about it; our big brain can say, "yeah, yeah, yeah, everything is impermanent," but meanwhile we are clinging on to whatever.
The second view is the view that true satisfaction can be found in things or ideas.
Let's go back to the four noble truths; the false view that you can get satisfaction out of something like that.
The third upside-down view is that there is a separate self.
The fourth upside-down view is that because something is attractive, it is not worth striving for and clinging to; that is a false view, it is not worth it.
The idea here is not that the bodhisattvas go to therapy for a long time and realize that they were mistaken and get new views that are smarter views.

The idea is that when we are really deeply in what relationship, feeling deeply about emptiness, connected to emptiness, in harmony with emptiness, that when that is true, these views just would not come up.
You would not think this.
Sometimes they use funny little metaphors, like saying it is like thinking of a winged rabbit.
You would not think of that, right?
Did you ever think of a winged rabbit before?
No, because there is no such thing.
And yet we think about all kinds of things which are not true either, as real as a winged rabbit, getting a lot of satisfaction for something that attracts us.
We can still enjoy things, but in a different way, right?
A softer way, a more open way, an appreciative way in the light of emptiness.
Once we are beyond all these inverted views, they just do not arise; they non-arise.
One realizes nirvana.
I am not sure if "realize" is quite the best translation there, but I did not get around to looking it up.
Nirvana is a traditional Buddhist term meaning peace, so one realizes true peace.
We can unpack that in a lot of ways, but let us keep moving.
When we really appreciate emptiness, we recognize there is nothing I need to do or get, or attain, and I can trust.
Relying on prajnaparamita you could also say is trusting, and then my mind is not messed up; we are okay, we are peaceful, we are not upside down.
The next paragraph seems to more or less be a sell job.
This is such a good way to go that Buddhas do it this way.
Do you not want to do it this way, as good as the Buddhas?

Not just any Buddha, all Buddhas, every single one—past, present, and future, every possible Buddha—relies on this, relies on prajnaparamita, and thereby attains unsurpassed, complete, perfect enlightenment.
Enlightenment is a bit of a troublemaker in our tradition.

On the one hand, it is a beautiful thing because it offers a sense of vision, like, "wow, we could be much bigger, happier," whatever that you can possibly imagine, and even more than that, it is all empty, so beyond anything you can think.
But then it sounds like something you would want to attain.
Exactly.
So what the heck?
In fact, there is the word, "attain."
So with nothing to attain, Buddhas attain.
It seems very paradoxical.
I do not know what the best way to think about enlightenment is.
It can encourage you, and it can mess you up because whatever you might think that it is, it cannot be that, right?
We know that, right?
It cannot be a view; it cannot be something you can conceptualize because that is the nature of emptiness.
The true reality is beyond anything we can put concepts and words to.
So the word enlightenment is just a pointer, a finger pointing to the moon, they say, just like emptiness is a pointer to something.
Maybe the best way to leave it for now is to have a big vision.
You think that is big?
No, go bigger.
Have a big, big vision for your life and our world, and practice that way.
Unsurpassed, complete, perfect enlightenment is actually a literal translation of a particular kind of meditation state, but it is the best one.
It is called Anyutara Samyaksambodhi.
When I first was practicing, the Heart Sutra had that untranslated, so I always think of those wonderful little Sanskrit phrase, Anyutara Samyaksambodhi.
It makes me happy to think about that.
Okay, so now another big pivot.
The Sanskrit does have a word that means basically "therefore."
Therefore, know the Prajnaparamita as the great miraculous mantra.
Do you ever notice how weird that is?

After all this kind of logical argumentation and doctrine and deep Buddhist philosophy and all about how there is nothing to attain and we are all completely free, therefore, these teachings really can be boiled down to a mantra, and not just any old mantra, a really good mantra: the Great Bright Mantra, the Supreme Mantra, the Incomparable Mantra.
There are all these traditional commentaries about why they picked exactly those adjectives, which do not matter right now.
This mantra is so powerful, it removes all suffering, and it is true, not false.
This is pretty interesting.
How do we suddenly get here?
Well, mantras, emerging from the spirituality of India in which Buddha started all this, are a deep and ancient practice.
The use of sound and also gesture, mudra and mantra, are connected words to express something that cannot be expressed in words.
Maybe it does fit the idea of emptiness, right?
Emptiness is pointing to the reality being bigger than words, so mantras are sounds that cannot be translated into words.
Sometimes there are actual words in there, but it is about the sounds.

One ancient commentary I read said the mantra is there for the really advanced students; they do not have to read the first part; they just need the mantra, and then they will understand the whole thing.
It said, for mid-level students like us, we need the whole thing and the mantra, and everybody else cannot understand this anyway, so do not worry about them.
But what the mantra does, though, is it provides a practice.
How do we practice no form, no feelings, no perceptions?
It is a non-practice, but a mantra is something that we can do, something we can embody, something we can express and put our heart energy into.
We can say the sounds of a mantra with great passion and energy, and something absolutely happens.
They are messing with us a little bit again here, kind of like what cannot be attained should be attained.
"True" and "false" would seem like concepts that do not make any sense in the light of emptiness, right?
Because they sound fixed in emptiness, and saying that nothing is fixed.
What is going on here?
None of the commentators seem to quite know why they said "true" and not "false."
Perhaps it is just to cheer us up, that it is really good stuff, I guess.
It is so powerful, it frees us completely, one hundred percent.
It removes all suffering.
Therefore, there is actually no more need for the Four Noble Truths because there is no suffering there that needs to be processed in that way.
Therefore, we proclaim.
Just say the mantra.

Maybe it is kind of like you sit through a lot of long lectures, like you have had to do here, sorry, and in the end, the teacher is just like, "yeah, forget all about that stuff; just fill in the blank; just be happy; just proclaim the mantra; just do whatever the thing is; just do it."
So therefore, we proclaim the Prajnaparamita Mantra, the mantra that says, *gate, gate, para gate, parasam gate, bodhi svaha*.
This is really about the power of sound.
There is also meaning in this particular gate, this particular mantra.
"Gate" means gone, like gone beyond.
"Para" and "parasam" are modifiers to "gate," so literally it means something like "gone, gone, gone beyond, completely beyond, awakening."
"Svaha" at the end does not literally mean "yes," but that is the spirit of it; it is kind of an exhalation, it is actually kind of an onomatopoeic word; it just means the sound, "Svaha."
What else could that mean?
"Svaha."
What is interesting is this is chanted everywhere in Zen, every Zen center, every day.
How many millions of times has this been chanted?
Who knows?
It is used a little bit somewhere or other, but basically it is not a systematic part of Zen practice to chant the Heart Sutra mantra, which does not stop you from chanting it.
I recommend it.
Maybe when you are out hiking on your own or something, you could chant this as you walk, "Parasam gate," and maybe it will really help you.
Maybe you chant it to yourself when things are really tough in your life.
"Gate, gate."
You have to wait a couple of days before you pass from this living world.
They boiled it down to a mantra, but then, for whatever reason, the mantra was not so much baked into Zen practice as we received it.
So there ends our version of the Heart Sutra.
Maybe you vaguely remember from a long time back there is a longer version that has a little frame story at the beginning and a conclusion at the end.
Here is the conclusion.
This version is chanted in Tibetan Buddhism, presumably was written in India.
After all this happened, remember the frame story from the beginning?
The Buddha is not mentioned at all in our version, but the Buddha is here.
The Buddha goes into a deep practice and inspires the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, the Bodhisattva of Compassion, and one of the Buddha's chief early students, to have a dialogue.
He inspires them both to have dialogue, and so essentially, through their voices, they are expressing the Buddha's teachings with Ananda teaching and Shariputra as a student.
The conclusion is then the Buddha rose from his concentration and complimented the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara Mahasattva, saying, "well done, well done, daughter of good family.
So it is, so it is.
Just as you have taught it, so should the deep perfection of wisdom be practiced.
Even the Tathagatas, the Buddhas, are full of joy.
Thus spoke the Buddha."

In raptured, the venerable Shariputra, the monk who was learning all this, in raptured, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, and the whole world with its gods, people, asuras, gandharvas, all kinds of creatures rejoiced in the Buddha's teaching.
That is the Heart Sutra; it is one way of looking at it.
Let us talk together about this.
Find yourself a trio in a minute.
We will take turns.
I will do the ringing the bell thing to keep the spaciousness, and just say whatever comes to mind.
If you are meaning this for the first time, who knows what you will say.
If you are meaning this for the millionth time, who knows what you will say.
What struck you?
What strikes you about the Heart Sutra?
What seems helpful or interesting or important or vexing or perplexing?
What comes up for you around these teachings?
What comes up in daily life that these teachings support you in?
Just see what comes up.
The beautiful, incredible possibility of getting to do a little trio work like that is that you get to listen to two other thoughtful people struggling with the same question.
We hold each other with grace and hold it all in confidence, and whatever you say is the perfect thing to say.
If you are not sure what to say, you can just say that and then sit a minute and see what comes.
It will be time turns, like three or four minutes.
If it is your turn, you really get the whole time.
If you do not want to say much more, you can just sit in silence; that is fine.
This crowd knows how to hang out with you in silence.
But maybe something else will bubble up.
In other words, it is not on the table to be like, "I am not really sure what to say, thanks, my turn is over, thanks, bye."
No, you still have your time.
Just be together.
There might be a group of four.
Try not to be in that group of four.
Let us try to have groups of three.

verbatim.text: One more talk on the Hartsutra, then I'll stop for now. First a side note, I hope you had a chance to greet our great first ancestor Bodhidharma on your way in. If you didn't notice him, he's standing patiently waiting for you, just kind of by the front door in the corner of the building. Donated, I don't even know the name of the donor actually, it was organized by her friend, named Steve Givens. Do you know Steve Givens? Oh, and I guess she is a collector of Asian art, and she moved away from Kent and wanted Bodhidharma to go to a good home. So check out Bodhidharma, it's pretty detailed carving, amazing carving, really beautiful. Carved out a one big piece of wood, and he's really heavy too.

And hopefully he's completed his journey, so now we can have a co-on. Why did Bodhidharma come from Kent? Now the red bearded barbarian. So some of you are here for some of the talks, or all of the talks maybe, on the Hartsutra, which we just chanted, the first of three. And fun, we're doing a couple more chants tonight than we have of late. And so we've already talked a lot about the central point of the sutra, which is to appreciate emptiness. This odd technical Buddhist term that translates as emptiness, which is a word that was used to point towards something much bigger than words.

The kind of wide open, interpenetrated, fluid way things actually are, unlike the way we tend to think they are without really thinking about the way we're thinking. We tend to lock things down, this is this, and this is that, and she's that way, and I'm this way. And we tend to assume that things are sort of inherently the way they are.
